scriptText:
Title: The Tide Clock
Author: Rough Cut release run

EXT. HARROWMERE HARBOUR - DAWN

Grey water fills a wide estuary. A stone causeway runs out from the harbour wall to a small island with a white schoolhouse.

On the harbour wall stands a tall clock tower of weathered brick, its face painted with the phases of the moon.

Fishing boats rock at their moorings. Gulls wheel over the nets.

A baker props open a shop door and sets out a tray of loaves to cool.

WREN ALDER, an apprentice clockmaker in a mustard scarf and a leather apron, runs along the harbour wall with a toolbag.

She stops beneath the tower and looks up. The minute hand trembles, then sticks.

Wren checks a brass pocket watch against the tower face. They disagree by four minutes.

WREN
Four minutes. Yesterday it was two.

She hurries to the tower door and unlocks it with a long iron key.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - DAWN - CONTINUOUS

A round room full of gears, pendulum weights and hanging tools. Dust turns in the light from a single window.

OSWIN FELL, the old clockmaker, white-haired and stooped, sits at a bench with a magnifying loupe on a cord around his neck.

He holds a small brass wheel close to his eye, then further away, squinting.

Wren sets down her toolbag and unrolls a canvas of tiny screwdrivers.

OSWIN
You heard it too.

WREN
The escapement is slipping. Four minutes since yesterday.

Oswin hands her the brass wheel. Its teeth are worn almost smooth.

Wren turns it in the window light. Her face falls.

Above them the great pendulum swings, slow and uneven.

A shelf of labelled drawers runs the length of the wall, each with a tiny brass handle.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - DAY

Wren climbs a ladder into the clock's works with a lantern in her teeth.

She watches the pallets catch and release the escape wheel. One pallet skips a tooth.

Close on the escape wheel: a tooth slides past where it should have caught.

Below, Oswin taps a chalkboard covered in tide tables.

OSWIN
The spring tide comes on the third night. The bell must ring true.

WREN
And if it rings late?

OSWIN
Then the night ferry crosses the causeway when the sea is already on it.

Wren climbs down and wipes oil from her hands, thinking.

She traces a column of figures on the chalkboard with one finger.

Oswin circles the third night on the tide table in red chalk.

EXT. CAUSEWAY - DAY

The stone causeway stretches across wet sand. Seaweed clings to its edges.

DEV MARSH, a ferryman's son in a blue knitted cap, pushes a handcart of lobster pots along it.

Wren catches up with him, out of breath.

DEV
You look like the clock ate your breakfast.

WREN
The clock is eating itself, Dev.

They stop at a tide post painted with white rings. The highest ring is far above their heads.

Dev knocks on the post. Water marks stain it up to the second ring.

Wren lays her palm flat against the highest ring and looks out at the open sea.

Far off, the schoolhouse bell on the island rings for morning lessons.

EXT. HARBOUR WALL - DAY

MARISOL QUAY, the harbour pilot, coils a rope beside her small green pilot boat. She wears a yellow oilskin and a captain's cap.

Wren and Dev approach along the wall.

Marisol does not look up from the rope.

MARISOL
Oswin's tower was slow at sunrise. I set my watch by it for thirty years.

WREN
Then you know what happens if it stops.

Marisol looks out at the causeway, then at the island.

She ties off the rope with one quick pull.

She taps the brass watch on her wrist and frowns at it.

INT. TOWN HALL - DAY

A long oak table under portraits of old harbour masters. Rain begins to tap the tall windows.

MAYOR HOLLIS, neat and tired, in a grey suit with a chain of office, reads a folded letter.

Wren and Oswin stand before the table. Oswin leans on a cane.

HOLLIS
The council has bought an electric siren. It arrives next month.

OSWIN
The tide arrives in three nights.

Hollis folds the letter and sets it beside a catalogue showing a siren on a steel mast.

Wren steps forward and lays the worn brass wheel on the table.

WREN
Give us three nights. We'll make it ring true.

Hollis turns the wheel over. He sighs and nods once.

A clerk at the end of the table writes the promise into a ledger.

INT. OSWIN'S COTTAGE - NIGHT

A cramped kitchen lit by an oil lamp. Clocks of every size tick on every wall.

Oswin pulls a wooden chest from under the stairs and opens it with trembling hands.

Inside lie rolled drawings tied with ribbon, and a leather notebook.

Wren unrolls a drawing on the table. It shows the tower clock in fine ink, signed by its maker.

Oswin taps a margin note with his loupe.

OSWIN
Agnes Penhallow built it. She made two of everything.

WREN
A spare escapement?

OSWIN
She kept it in the chapel on the sandbank. The sea took the chapel years ago.

Wren looks at the drawing, then at the dark window where the tide hisses on the shingle.

Every clock on the wall strikes ten together, then one more, a moment behind.

EXT. HARROWMERE HARBOUR - NIGHT

Lamps glow along the harbour wall. Dev sits on an upturned boat mending a net.

Wren walks up with the rolled drawing under her arm.

She unrolls it on the boat's hull and pins the corners with stones.

WREN
The old chapel on the sandbank. Can you get us there?

DEV
At low water, on the second morning. We would have an hour.

Dev ties a final knot and bites the twine.

Above them the tower clock strikes nine, a heartbeat late.

They both look up at it in silence.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - NIGHT

Wren works alone by lamplight, measuring the worn pallets with calipers.

She writes numbers in Agnes Penhallow's notebook beside the old ink.

The pendulum swings behind her. Its shadow sweeps the wall like a slow wave.

She holds the drawing up to the lamp and compares it with the works overhead.

She rests her head on her arms for a moment.

Her eyes close. The ticking fills the room.

The lamp gutters low.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - DAWN

Grey light through the window. Wren wakes at the bench with ink on her cheek.

Oswin stands at the door holding two mugs of tea.

OSWIN
You slept in the works. So did I, at your age.

Wren takes a mug and points to her figures.

WREN
If the spare pallets match these, we can fit them in a day.

Oswin peers at the page through his loupe, then nods slowly.

He lays a folded oilskin on the bench beside her.

EXT. HARBOUR WALL - DAWN

Marisol's pilot boat idles at the steps. Dev loads coils of rope, a lantern, and a canvas bag of tools.

Wren and Oswin come down the steps. Oswin stays on the bottom stair.

OSWIN
Bring back Agnes's work, not your own bones.

WREN
Both, I promise.

Marisol helps Wren aboard and casts off.

Oswin lifts his cane in farewell from the bottom stair.

The boat pulls away across flat silver water toward the sandbank.

EXT. ESTUARY - DAWN - MOVING

The pilot boat cuts a long wake. Mist lies low on the water.

Marisol steers by a compass in a brass binnacle. Dev watches the depth line.

DEV
Two fathoms. One and a half.

MARISOL
The bank is close. Watch for the bell tower.

A cormorant surfaces beside the hull and dives again.

Out of the mist rises a broken stone arch, crusted with barnacles.

Wren stands at the bow, holding the drawing against the wind.

EXT. SANDBANK - DAWN

The tide has drawn back. A ruined chapel stands half buried in wet sand, its windows full of weed.

The boat grounds gently. Dev jumps down and drives an anchor into the sand.

Marisol checks her watch and holds up one finger.

MARISOL
One hour. Then the sea wants this place back.

Wren climbs through a broken doorway with the lantern.

Dev follows, carrying a shovel.

Their footprints fill slowly with water behind them.

INT. RUINED CHAPEL - DAWN - CONTINUOUS

Green light falls through holes in the roof. Pools of seawater glitter on the stone floor.

Crabs scuttle away from the lantern beam.

Wren finds a stone shelf carved with a clock face, half hidden by weed.

She pulls the weed away. Behind it is a small iron door with a keyhole.

Dev tries the shovel blade in the seam. It will not move.

Wren holds up the long iron key from the tower. It fits.

The little door swings open with a groan.

INT. RUINED CHAPEL - DAWN - CONTINUOUS

Inside the niche sits a wooden box wrapped in waxed cloth.

Wren lifts it out and unwraps it on her knees.

A bright brass escapement lies in oiled felt, untouched by the sea.

DEV
It's like she wrapped it yesterday.

WREN
She knew someone would need it.

A folded note in faded ink is tucked under the felt. Wren slips it into her apron.

Water trickles across the floor toward their boots.

Dev looks back at the doorway. The light outside has changed.

EXT. SANDBANK - DAY

The sea is returning in thin silver channels across the sand.

Marisol stands knee deep beside the boat, hauling on the anchor line.

MARISOL
Now, both of you. Now.

Wren runs out holding the box against her chest. Dev splashes behind her.

They tumble into the boat. Marisol shoves off and jumps aboard.

The engine coughs, then catches.

The chapel doorway disappears under the first wave.

EXT. ESTUARY - DAY - MOVING

The pilot boat rides the incoming swell back toward Harrowmere.

Wren sits in the stern with the box on her lap, laughing with relief.

Dev wrings seawater out of his cap.

DEV
Next time you need a spare part, try a shop.

Marisol grins at the wheel.

Wren unfolds the faded note. It reads: for whoever keeps the tide.

Ahead, the clock tower rises over the harbour wall.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - DAY

Oswin waits at the bench. Wren sets the box before him and opens it.

He lifts the escapement into the window light and studies it through his loupe.

OSWIN
Agnes, you clever old soul.

Wren lays the worn part beside the new one. The difference is plain.

She lays Agnes's note beside them. Oswin reads it and smiles.

She tightens a vice and takes out her finest screwdriver.

Oswin hands her a tin of clock oil without a word.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - DAY - CONTINUOUS

Wren climbs into the works and stops the pendulum with both hands.

The ticking stops. The room is suddenly very quiet.

She unscrews the old pallet arbor and passes it down to Oswin.

Oswin wraps it in a cloth like something precious.

Wren seats the new escapement and tests it with one finger.

It ticks once, sharp and clean.

WREN
It fits.

OSWIN
Now make it keep time.

EXT. HARBOUR WALL - DAY

Townsfolk gather below the tower, pointing up at the stopped hands.

Hollis pushes through the small crowd under an umbrella.

HOLLIS
Why has the clock stopped?

MARISOL
Because it's being mended.

Hollis looks up at the tower window, where Wren's lamp is burning.

The baker hands out warm loaves to the waiting crowd.

He lowers his umbrella and waits with the rest.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - AFTERNOON

Wren releases the pendulum. It swings, and the escape wheel begins to turn.

Oswin holds the brass pocket watch beside his ear and counts under his breath.

Wren adjusts the pendulum bob a quarter turn.

OSWIN
Slow by a breath. Again.

She turns it once more and steps back.

Close on the escape wheel: each tooth catches and releases cleanly.

The hands move. The clock and the pocket watch agree.

Oswin closes his eyes and smiles.

EXT. HARROWMERE HARBOUR - SUNSET

The tower clock strikes six, clear across the water.

On the harbour wall, the townsfolk look up and clap.

Dev whistles from his boat. Marisol raises her cap.

Hollis checks his own watch, then looks up at the tower, surprised.

He winds his watch forward to match the tower.

In the tower window, Wren waves, oil on her hands.

INT. OSWIN'S COTTAGE - NIGHT

The oil lamp burns low. Oswin and Wren eat bread and soup at the kitchen table.

Agnes Penhallow's notebook lies open between them.

OSWIN
The spring tide is tomorrow night. The flood bell must ring at the turn.

WREN
I'll sit with it all night.

Oswin reaches across and squeezes her hand.

Wren tucks Agnes's note into the back of the notebook.

Outside, the wind rises and rattles the shutters.

EXT. HARROWMERE HARBOUR - NIGHT

A storm gathers over the estuary. Rain sweeps across the lamps.

The moored boats strain at their lines.

Wren hurries along the wall in her oilskin, the long key in her fist.

Dev runs to meet her, shouting over the wind.

DEV
The ferry left the island early. It's on the causeway now.

Wren stares out into the dark, where a single ferry lantern bobs on the causeway.

A wave breaks over the harbour wall and sprays them both.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - NIGHT

Wren bursts in, soaked. The pendulum swings steadily.

She checks the tide tables on the chalkboard against the clock face.

The hands stand at a minute to the hour, exactly on time.

The flood bell lever is tied back with an old rope.

WREN
It isn't the clock. The bell rope is fouled.

She climbs the ladder toward the belfry, rain pouring through the shutters.

EXT. CLOCK TOWER BELFRY - NIGHT

Wind howls through the open arches. The great bronze flood bell hangs still.

Wren reaches the bell frame and finds the rope wedged in a split beam.

She pulls with all her weight. It does not move.

Below, through the rain, the ferry lantern crawls along the causeway.

Wren braces her boots against the frame and pulls again.

The rope tears free. She falls back against the beam, holding it.

EXT. CLOCK TOWER BELFRY - NIGHT - CONTINUOUS

The clock strikes the hour below her. The bell lever trembles.

Wren hauls the rope hand over hand.

The great bell swings. Its first stroke booms across the estuary.

She rings it again and again, rain streaming down her face.

WREN
Turn back. Turn back.

Lights come on in windows all along the harbour.

EXT. CAUSEWAY - NIGHT

The ferry lantern stops halfway across. Water already washes over the stones.

The FERRYMAN, a stout figure in a sou'wester, raises the lantern toward the sound.

He turns the horse and cart around on the narrow causeway.

Passengers huddle under blankets as the cart rolls back toward the island.

The horse finds its footing on the wet stones, step by careful step.

Behind them, the sea pours over the causeway where they had been.

EXT. HARBOUR WALL - NIGHT

Marisol and Dev watch the ferry lantern retreat to the island.

Townsfolk crowd the wall in coats and nightclothes, listening to the bell.

Hollis stands among them, bareheaded in the rain.

HOLLIS
That bell has done what no siren could.

MARISOL
It always has, Mayor.

Dev lets out a long breath and grins at Marisol.

The bell falls quiet. The storm begins to ease.

INT. CLOCK TOWER BELFRY - NIGHT

Wren sits against the bell frame, exhausted, the rope still in her hands.

Footsteps on the ladder. Oswin climbs up slowly, lantern first.

He sits beside her and listens to the clock ticking below.

OSWIN
Agnes would have liked you.

Wren rests her head on his shoulder.

The rain thins to a drizzle, then stops.

Through the arches, the clouds break over a full moon.

EXT. HARROWMERE HARBOUR - DAWN

Calm water. The causeway emerges from the ebbing tide, glistening.

The ferry cart rolls across from the island, passengers waving.

Dev and Marisol wave back from the pilot boat.

The baker opens the shop door and sets out the morning loaves.

The tower clock strikes seven, exactly on time.

INT. TOWN HALL - DAY

Sunlight fills the long room. The siren catalogue lies closed at the end of the table.

Hollis signs a letter and blots it.

HOLLIS
The council will keep the tower clock. And its keepers.

Oswin and Wren stand before the table. Oswin nods his thanks.

The clerk underlines the promise in the ledger.

Hollis pushes the siren catalogue into a drawer and shuts it.

INT. CLOCK TOWER WORKSHOP - DAY

Oswin takes the loupe on its cord from around his neck.

He places it over Wren's head and settles it on her apron.

OSWIN
The tower is yours to keep now.

WREN
Ours. You still have to tell me when I'm slow.

Oswin laughs. Wren lifts the loupe to her eye and studies the escape wheel.

She pins Agnes's note above the bench, beside the tide tables.

EXT. HARROWMERE HARBOUR - SUNSET

The whole estuary glows gold. The tower clock face catches the last light.

Wren stands on the harbour wall beside Oswin, Dev and Marisol.

Out on the island, the schoolhouse windows shine in the low sun.

The clock strikes the hour, and gulls lift from the water.

The camera rises past the clock face to the open sky.

FADE OUT.

styleBible.look: Go soft and painterly: cool silver-grey dawns, amber lamplight in the workshop, deep teal storm night, then a golden sunset finish. Give special treatment to the escape wheel close-ups, the green-lit chapel, the belfry bell swing, and the final rise past the clock face to the sky.
